opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, for most of us inside, it came as a complete surprise. I found out at roughly the same time as everyone else: a message went around, people started checking their phones, and the first reaction was simply, "Wait, what? Is this real?" There was no warning at the level where most of us worked. We were just doing our jobs, training models, fixing bugs, and suddenly the CEO was gone.

The first day or two were very confusing, because nobody had a clear explanation. The board's statement was vague. Internally, people kept asking, "What exactly happened? Was there some serious wrongdoing?" Without a concrete answer, people filled the gap with speculation, and that made things more tense.

What I remember most is how quickly the company came together. Within a very short time, almost everyone signed the letter saying that if things weren't resolved, we would follow Sam. For me, that wasn't really about worshipping one person. It was about the team and the mission. Many of us felt that what we had built was working really well, and that a decision like this, made with so little explanation, put all of it at risk. People cared about keeping the group together more than about any single position.

Looking back, I think it showed a real tension that exists at a place like OpenAI. On one side, there's the nonprofit structure and the board's responsibility for safety and governance, which is a legitimate concern. On the other side, there's a very fast-moving organization where people trust each other and want to keep shipping. When those two sides don't communicate well, you get a crisis like that.

So my understanding from the inside was less about the boardroom politics, which I honestly didn't know much about, and more about what it revealed: how much the people there cared, and how fragile governance can be when the stakes are this high. It was a stressful few days, but in a strange way it also made the team feel closer afterward.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, from the inside it felt just as sudden as it looked from the outside. I remember it was a Friday, and I was going about a normal workday when the news came out. There was no warning, no internal memo beforehand. Most of us found out basically at the same time as everyone on Twitter did.

My first reaction was confusion more than anything. The board's statement was very vague, something about Sam not being consistently candid, and nobody could really explain what that meant concretely. So you had hundreds of employees trying to piece things together from the same public information everyone else had, plus whatever rumors were going around on Slack.

What struck me most over that weekend was how quickly the company came together. The vast majority of employees signed that open letter saying they would leave if the board didn't reverse the decision. That wasn't something leadership forced on people. It came from the bottom up, because people genuinely trusted Sam and Greg and felt the board had acted without a clear justification. There was also a lot of practical worry. OpenAI was moving extremely fast at that point, and the idea that everything could just fall apart over a weekend was kind of terrifying.

In hindsight I think it exposed a structural problem rather than a personal one. The nonprofit board had enormous formal power but very little connection to the people actually building things, and when the two sides disagreed there was no good mechanism to resolve it. Once Sam came back and the board was reconstituted, I think most people just wanted to get back to work. But it definitely changed how a lot of us thought about governance and how fragile that whole setup had been.
